questions.question: What is the primary management-architecture difference between a traditional on-premises managed network and a cloud-managed network (e.g., Cisco Meraki)?
choices: On-premises devices cannot be managed remotely at all
Cloud-managed devices send configuration and telemetry to a vendor-hosted dashboard accessed over the internet, instead of a locally hosted controller
Cloud-managed networks do not support VLANs
On-premises networks cannot use SNMP
questions.explanation: Cloud-based management moves the management plane (dashboard, configuration database, analytics) to a vendor-hosted cloud service reached over the internet, versus a locally hosted controller or per-device CLI/SNMP management on-prem.

correct.explanation: Cloud-managed gear phones home to a vendor-hosted dashboard over the internet — config and telemetry centralize off-box.

incorrect.explanation: On-prem devices can be managed remotely via SNMP/SSH — the difference is where the controller lives.
incorrect.whatItDoes: On-premises devices cannot be managed remotely at all points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud vs local management.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud vs local management", Cloud-managed devices send configuration and telemetry to a vendor-hosted dashboard accessed over the internet, instead of a locally hosted controller satisfies what this question tests — On-premises devices cannot be managed remotely at all does not.

incorrect.explanation: Cloud platforms support VLANs — architecture differs in controller placement, not L2 features.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Cloud-managed networks do not support VLANs points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud vs local management.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud vs local management", Cloud-managed devices send configuration and telemetry to a vendor-hosted dashboard accessed over the internet, instead of a locally hosted controller satisfies what this question tests — Cloud-managed networks do not support VLANs does not.

incorrect.explanation: On-prem networks commonly use SNMP — cloud adds a hosted orchestration layer.
incorrect.whatItDoes: On-premises networks cannot use SNMP points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud vs local management.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud vs local management", Cloud-managed devices send configuration and telemetry to a vendor-hosted dashboard accessed over the internet, instead of a locally hosted controller satisfies what this question tests — On-premises networks cannot use SNMP does not.

answerReview.examTip: Cloud-managed = devices → vendor cloud dashboard; on-prem = local NMS/controller.

questions.question: A company with 50 branch offices wants a single dashboard to monitor and configure all branch switches and APs without establishing a VPN to each site individually. Which management approach best fits this requirement?
choices: Local CLI management via console cable at each site
A cloud-based management platform (e.g., Meraki dashboard)
SNMPv1 polling from a central NMS
Telnet to each device's management IP
questions.explanation: Cloud-based management platforms are designed for exactly this scenario: centralized, single-pane-of-glass visibility and configuration across many geographically distributed sites without per-site VPN tunnels.

correct.explanation: Cloud-based management platforms are designed for exactly this scenario: centralized, single-pane-of-glass visibility and configuration across many geographically distributed sites without per-site VPN tunnels.

incorrect.explanation: Console at each of 50 branches does not scale — cloud dashboard provides centralized monitor/configure without traveling to every site.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Choosing per-site console for multi-branch management
incorrect.whatItDoes: Local CLI management via console cable at each site points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud management use case.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud management use case", A cloud-based management platform (e.g., Meraki dashboard) satisfies what this question tests — Local CLI management via console cable at each site does not.

incorrect.explanation: SNMPv1 polling is read-heavy and lacks unified push config — cloud platforms provide dashboard config plus monitoring across all branches.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting SNMPv1 alone to replace cloud dashboard
incorrect.whatItDoes: SNMPv1 polling from a central NMS points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud management use case.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud management use case", A cloud-based management platform (e.g., Meraki dashboard) satisfies what this question tests — SNMPv1 polling from a central NMS does not.

incorrect.explanation: Telnet to each device is insecure and unscalable — cloud management avoids per-site VPN and manual CLI on 50 branches.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using Telnet per device for 50-site management
incorrect.whatItDoes: Telnet to each device's management IP uses cleartext Telnet for remote device management.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Device management (cloud management use case): A cloud-based management platform (e.g., Meraki dashboard) protects credentials in transit — Telnet to each device's management IP uses cleartext remote access.

answerReview.examTip: Fleet-wide template push → cloud controller (DNA Center class).

questions.question: An organization's cloud-managed access points lose connectivity to the cloud dashboard during an ISP outage at headquarters. What is the most accurate description of the impact on the branch network?
choices: All wireless clients are immediately disconnected
The APs typically continue forwarding existing traffic (data plane unaffected), but configuration changes and cloud analytics are unavailable until connectivity is restored
The APs factory-reset themselves automatically
Wired switches in the same branch also stop forwarding traffic
questions.explanation: Most cloud-managed architectures separate the data plane (local forwarding continues independently) from the management/control plane (cloud dashboard). A WAN/internet outage interrupts management visibility and configuration push, but local forwarding generally continues using the last-known configuration.
questions.concept: cloud management data vs control plane

correct.explanation: Cloud-managed APs usually keep forwarding locally (data plane) but lose dashboard management, config push, and analytics until WAN returns.

incorrect.explanation: Clients typically stay connected — local forwarding continues; only cloud management/control is interrupted.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Assuming total wireless outage when cloud link drops
incorrect.whatItDoes: All wireless clients are immediately disconnected points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud management data vs control plane.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud management data vs control plane", The APs typically continue forwarding existing traffic (data plane unaffected), but configuration changes and cloud analytics are unavailable until connectivity is restored satisfies what this question tests — All wireless clients are immediately disconnected does not.

incorrect.explanation: APs do not factory-reset on WAN loss — they run last-known config and resume cloud sync when connectivity returns.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting automatic factory reset on management outage
incorrect.whatItDoes: The APs factory-reset themselves automatically points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud management data vs control plane.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud management data vs control plane", The APs typically continue forwarding existing traffic (data plane unaffected), but configuration changes and cloud analytics are unavailable until connectivity is restored satisfies what this question tests — The APs factory-reset themselves automatically does not.

incorrect.explanation: Wired switch forwarding is independent — the scenario describes cloud AP management loss, not wired data-plane failure.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Extending AP management outage to wired switching
incorrect.whatItDoes: Wired switches in the same branch also stop forwarding traffic points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for cloud management data vs control plane.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "cloud management data vs control plane", The APs typically continue forwarding existing traffic (data plane unaffected), but configuration changes and cloud analytics are unavailable until connectivity is restored satisfies what this question tests — Wired switches in the same branch also stop forwarding traffic does not.

answerReview.examTip: Cloud WAN down → local forwarding continues; management/analytics pause.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical advantage of cloud-based device management over traditional local management?
choices: Lower latency for all management operations regardless of internet connectivity
Zero-touch provisioning — new devices can be shipped to a site and automatically pull their configuration from the cloud on first boot
No internet connection is ever required
Configuration changes never require any internet access
questions.explanation: A hallmark benefit of cloud management is zero-touch provisioning: a device shipped to a remote site can connect to the internet, phone home to the cloud controller, and automatically receive its configuration — no on-site CLI work needed.

correct.explanation: Zero-touch provisioning (ZTP) lets new devices auto-pull config from the cloud on first boot — no console visit required.

incorrect.explanation: Cloud management depends on internet reachability — it does not guarantee lower latency than local CLI.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Lower latency for all management operations regardless of internet connectivity points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for zero-touch provisioning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "zero-touch provisioning", Zero-touch provisioning — new devices can be shipped to a site and automatically pull their configuration from the cloud on first boot satisfies what this question tests — Lower latency for all management operations regardless of internet connectivity does not.

incorrect.explanation: Cloud management requires internet for dashboard control — not zero connectivity.
incorrect.whatItDoes: No internet connection is ever required points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for zero-touch provisioning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "zero-touch provisioning", Zero-touch provisioning — new devices can be shipped to a site and automatically pull their configuration from the cloud on first boot satisfies what this question tests — No internet connection is ever required does not.

incorrect.explanation: Pushing policy from the cloud needs connectivity — ZTP is the benefit, not offline-only operation.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Configuration changes never require any internet access points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for zero-touch provisioning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "zero-touch provisioning", Zero-touch provisioning — new devices can be shipped to a site and automatically pull their configuration from the cloud on first boot satisfies what this question tests — Configuration changes never require any internet access does not.

answerReview.examTip: Meraki/cloud win: ZTP, centralized monitoring, fleet firmware — trade-off = cloud dependency.

questions.question: From a security/compliance standpoint, what is a common reason an organization might prefer local (on-premises) device management over cloud-based management?

Management traffic and configuration data stay entirely within the organization's own network rather than transiting a third-party cloud provider
Local management doesn't require any administrator training
Local management automatically encrypts all user data
questions.explanation: Some organizations (e.g., due to regulatory or data-sovereignty requirements) prefer on-premises management because configuration and telemetry data never leaves their own infrastructure or transits a third-party cloud.

correct.explanation: Local management keeps config and management traffic inside the org network — no third-party cloud transit.

incorrect.explanation: Local isn't always faster — the driver is data sovereignty and compliance, not speed.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Local management is always faster to configure points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for on-prem management security rationale.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "on-prem management security rationale", Management traffic and configuration data stay entirely within the organization's own network rather than transiting a third-party cloud provider satisfies what this question tests — Local management is always faster to configure does not.

incorrect.explanation: Both models require trained administrators — local doesn't eliminate training.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Local management doesn't require any administrator training points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for on-prem management security rationale.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "on-prem management security rationale", Management traffic and configuration data stay entirely within the organization's own network rather than transiting a third-party cloud provider satisfies what this question tests — Local management doesn't require any administrator training does not.

incorrect.explanation: Local management doesn't automatically encrypt user data — that's a separate security control.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Local management automatically encrypts all user data points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for on-prem management security rationale.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "on-prem management security rationale", Management traffic and configuration data stay entirely within the organization's own network rather than transiting a third-party cloud provider satisfies what this question tests — Local management automatically encrypts all user data does not.

answerReview.examTip: Local vs cloud: compliance/sovereignty favors on-prem | scale/automation favors cloud.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical characteristic of traditional local (on-premises) network management?
choices: Devices are managed individually via CLI, SNMP, or a locally-hosted controller, often requiring per-site or per-device access
All configuration is pushed automatically from a vendor's global cloud

Management is impossible without a dedicated WAN link to each branch
questions.explanation: Traditional on-premises management typically means administrators connect to each device (or a locally hosted controller) individually via CLI, SNMP, or a local management application — less centralized than cloud dashboards.

correct.explanation: Traditional local management uses per-device CLI, SNMP, or on-site controllers — often site-by-site access.

incorrect.explanation: Vendor global cloud push describes cloud-managed — not traditional local.
incorrect.whatItDoes: All configuration is pushed automatically from a vendor's global cloud points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for local management characteristics.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "local management characteristics", Devices are managed individually via CLI, SNMP, or a locally-hosted controller, often requiring per-site or per-device access satisfies what this question tests — All configuration is pushed automatically from a vendor's global cloud does not.

incorrect.explanation: Automatic fleet firmware from vendor cloud is cloud-managed lifecycle.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Firmware updates are applied automatically across all sites with no administrator involvement points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for local management characteristics.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "local management characteristics", Devices are managed individually via CLI, SNMP, or a locally-hosted controller, often requiring per-site or per-device access satisfies what this question tests — Firmware updates are applied automatically across all sites with no administrator involvement does not.

incorrect.explanation: Local management doesn't require WAN to every branch — on-site access works.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Management is impossible without a dedicated WAN link to each branch points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for local management characteristics.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "local management characteristics", Devices are managed individually via CLI, SNMP, or a locally-hosted controller, often requiring per-site or per-device access satisfies what this question tests — Management is impossible without a dedicated WAN link to each branch does not.

questions.question: A cloud-managed network platform automatically pushes firmware updates to all devices in an organization on a scheduled maintenance window from the vendor's cloud. What management capability does this best illustrate?

questions.explanation: Centralized firmware/lifecycle management — pushing updates to many devices across many sites from one cloud console — is a defining capability of cloud-managed architectures, reducing manual per-device maintenance.

correct.explanation: Scheduled cloud-pushed firmware across the fleet = centralized automated lifecycle management.

incorrect.explanation: CLI scripting is manual/local — not automated cloud fleet updates.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Local CLI scripting applies another routing protocol's behavior instead of OSPF-specific rules.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "centralized lifecycle management", Centralized, automated lifecycle management across the fleet from a single cloud platform satisfies what this question tests — Local CLI scripting does not.

incorrect.explanation: Per-device TFTP is manual — cloud platforms push centrally scheduled updates.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Manual per-device firmware upload via TFTP points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for centralized lifecycle management.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "centralized lifecycle management", Centralized, automated lifecycle management across the fleet from a single cloud platform satisfies what this question tests — Manual per-device firmware upload via TFTP does not.

incorrect.explanation: VLAN trunking is Layer 2 config — not firmware lifecycle management.
incorrect.whatItDoes: VLAN trunking configuration expects VLAN tags on a link that should behave as access-only in this stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "centralized lifecycle management", Centralized, automated lifecycle management across the fleet from a single cloud platform satisfies what this question tests — VLAN trunking configuration does not.

answerReview.examTip: Cloud management wins: firmware orchestration, template config, multi-site visibility.

incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "single pane of glass", A single user interface or dashboard provides visibility and control over the entire network's devices and sites satisfies what this question tests — All devices share one physical management cable does not.

incorrect.whatItDoes: Only one administrator account exists for the whole network points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for single pane of glass.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "single pane of glass", A single user interface or dashboard provides visibility and control over the entire network's devices and sites satisfies what this question tests — Only one administrator account exists for the whole network does not.

incorrect.explanation: Devices can be geographically distributed — one dashboard still unifies them.

incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "single pane of glass", A single user interface or dashboard provides visibility and control over the entire network's devices and sites satisfies what this question tests — All devices are physically located in the same rack does not.
